tier_reason: The independent lzbench 2.4 table (public code, inikep/lzbench; gcc 15.2.0 release binary; single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P, turbo off, silesia.tar) lists brieflz 1.3.0 -6 at 22.8 / 328 MB/s, 31.71% vs zlib 1.3.2 -9 at 11.3 / 318 MB/s, 31.92%; compile flags are not stated on the README, so B, consistent with other lzbench-based entries in this wave. The BriefLZ README table (17 / 400 vs 11 / 320 MB/s, Core i5-4570) matches the record but is first-party with no compiler or flags.

corrections.caveats: Decompression gain over zlib is marginal (3% in lzbench 2.4, 25% in the 2020 README table). At matched levels the picture is mixed: brieflz -6 (22.8 MB/s, 31.71%) compresses slower than zlib -6 (26.8 MB/s, 32.19%) for a 1.5% smaller output; the clear wins are brieflz -6 vs zlib -9 and brieflz -3 (124 / 301 MB/s, 35.65%) vs zlib -1 (89.0 / 297 MB/s, 36.45%), derived from page data. The README says its comparison 'is not entirely fair because BriefLZ has no window size limit'. zstd and brotli beat it at similar ratios, and zlib-ng/libdeflate are not compared. Tier B rests on the third-party lzbench 2.4 table; the README table is first-party and lacks compiler flags.

notes: All quoted numbers match both pages. benchmark_url moved to the lzbench README, which carries the tier-B evidence; the BriefLZ README remains the first-party source. Last commit 2024-02-02 (CI update), 111 stars, Zlib license, not a fork.

tier_reason: The independent lzbench 2.4 table (public code, gcc 15.2.0 release binary, -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4, single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P, silesia.tar) lists brotli 1.2.0 -5 at 53.3 / 419 MB/s, 28.10% vs zlib 1.3.2 -9 at 11.3 / 318 MB/s, 31.92% and xz 5.8.4 -1 at 19.2 / 105 MB/s, 27.75%; compile flags are not on the README, so B rather than A.
notes: All numbers and derived ratios check out (4.7x / 1.3x vs zlib -9; 2.8x / 4.0x vs xz -1 at 1.3% larger output). Brotli was NOT on data/known_list.txt before this wave's w9-lossless-registry merge (it appears now only because merge.py added this record); it is a named baseline of general-lossless in spec Part 4, so the orchestrator may prefer to file it as a category incumbent rather than a faster-than entry. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 14.9k stars, last commit 2026-09-30.

tier_reason: The lzbench 2.4 table (public code, gcc 15.2.0 release binary, single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P, silesia.tar), run by the lzbench maintainer, lists lbzip2 2.6.5 -1 at 22.0 / 62.7 MB/s vs bzip2 1.0.8 -1 at 13.5 / 41.1 MB/s and -9 at 22.4 / 47.0 vs 12.7 / 35.5 MB/s; flags not on the README, so B. The fork's own README table (M5 Max, -O3, vs lbzip2 2.5) is first-party.

corrections.caveats: Baseline bzip2 is not in this category's list. The fork was created on 2026-08-17 from upstream commit 724352c and is one person's work (1 star). The lzbench CHANGELOG credits the lbzip2 2.6.5 integration to @caius72 (the fork author), although the table itself was run by the lzbench maintainer. Gain in the lzbench table is a single-thread comparison; most of the gain over bzip2 comes from upstream lbzip2's BWT/MTF implementation, and the fork itself adds about 8-9% over lbzip2 2.5 (first-party, Apple M5 Max). GPL-3.0-or-later.

notes: Numbers match the lzbench 2.4 row. On folding: upstream kjn/lbzip2 (156 stars, GPL-3.0, not archived) is not on the known list, so this maintained fork does not fold into a listed project; it is effectively the lbzip2 entry, and the orchestrator could note kjn/lbzip2 as the original. GitHub marks it as a fork of kjn/lbzip2; last commit 2026-08-19.
